title: Nonlinear Hall effect in Floquet-driven monolayer 1T$'$-MoS$_2$
authors: Muhammad Faisal, Muzamil Shah, Imtiaz Khan, Reza Asgari
abstract: We study the nonlinear Hall effect in Floquet-driven monolayer \(1T'\)-MoS\(_2\), a low-symmetry quantum spin Hall material whose tilted Dirac bands sustain an intrinsic Berry-curvature dipole without the need for strain or trigonal warping. We show that off-resonant circularly polarized light offers a way to control both the sign and the magnitude of the nonlinear Hall response through optically induced topological phase transitions using a Floquet effective Hamiltonian and nonlinear semiclassical transport theory. We show that the anisotropic crystal symmetry enforces a selection rule in which the Berry-curvature dipole elements satisfy $D_x\equiv0$, while a finite $D_y$ originates from the intrinsic band tilt. The Berry curvature is recreated in momentum space as the Floquet drive successively inverts individual spin-valley sectors, resulting in an identical sign reversal of the nonlinear Hall conductivity and the Berry-curvature dipole at each bulk gap closing. In contrast, tuning the band tilt modifies only the magnitude of the response without changing its sign, establishing the observed sign reversal as an unambiguous transport signature of genuine Floquet topological phase transitions. We further show that the nonlinear Hall response can be controlled by the driving strength, perpendicular electric field, Fermi energy, and temperature, providing multiple experimental knobs for observation. Our findings establish the sign of the nonlinear Hall response as a universal transport fingerprint of Floquet-engineered topology and point to monolayer \(1T'\)-MoS\(_2\) as a viable platform for all-electrical detection of nonequilibrium topological phases.
summary: This work investigates the nonlinear Hall effect in Floquet-driven 1T'-MoS2 to characterize engineered topological phases. The key finding is that a sign reversal in the NHE conductivity provides an unambiguous signature of these transitions, distinguishing them from simple parameter tuning. This establishes the material as a viable platform for all-electrical detection of non-equilibrium topology.
main_problem: The study aims to establish a universal transport fingerprint for Floquet-engineered topology by investigating the nonlinear Hall effect (NHE) in driven 2D materials.
main_result: A sign reversal in the NHE conductivity, which coincides with optically induced band inversions and gap closings, serves as an unambiguous signature of genuine topological phase transitions.
method: The analysis employs a high-frequency Floquet effective Hamiltonian derived from coupling to circularly polarized light and utilizes nonlinear semiclassical transport theory.
model_or_system: The system is monolayer 1T'-MoS2, modeled as a low-symmetry quantum spin Hall material with intrinsic Berry-curvature dipole moments. The driving mechanism involves off-resonant circularly polarized light applied via minimal coupling.
key_observables: Nonlinear Hall conductivity (chi_xyy), Berry-curvature dipole moment (D_y), and the total Chern number of the occupied band.
important_parameters: Floquet drive strength ($\xi$), perpendicular electric field ($E_z$, controlled by $\alpha$), Fermi energy ($E_F$), and temperature ($T$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the off-resonant high-frequency (van Vleck) expansion for the Floquet effective Hamiltonian.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how D_y changes sign only when the gap closes due to driving ($\xi$), contrasting this with monotonic changes observed when tuning band tilt or electric field alone. Temperature dependence shows signal suppression at higher T.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the model and Hamiltonian, then calculates topological invariants (Chern number) under Floquet driving. The core argument links sign reversals in the Berry-curvature dipole moment to these topological phase transitions, demonstrating this link via the NHE measurement, and finally explores control knobs like electric field and temperature.
why_interesting: The use of non-equilibrium optical driving to induce and probe topological phases is highly relevant for AMO physics, particularly concerning how external fields (like light) can engineer quantum states in solid-state systems.
